# SK2063 — The operator sequence reads as a different operator

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `=` is written hard against a following unary `-`, `+` or `!` and separated from the operand — `x =- 1` — so the pair reads as the compound operator `-=` and is not one.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S2757 |

## Why

`x =- 1` assigns negative one. `x -= 1` subtracts one. C# has no `=-` operator, so the compiler splits the two characters silently and the reader's eye does not. ⚠ **The whitespace is the entire signal, and it is the only signal there is.** `x = -1` and `x =- 1` are the same program and differ only in layout, so nothing semantic can separate the deliberate from the mistyped; what separates them is that somebody wrote the `=` and the sign as one token and then put a space before the number, which is how `-=` is spelled and not how a negative literal is. A rule that ignored trivia here would have nothing left to look at.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
remaining =- 1;
```

Write:

```csharp
remaining -= 1;

// or, if assignment really was meant, written so it reads that way:
remaining = -1;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Three conditions must hold together, and each one alone would over-fire.** The `=` and the unary operator must be adjacent with no trivia between them; the unary operator must be separated from its operand by trivia; and there must be trivia before the `=`. `x = -1` (spaced normally), `x =-1` (both halves closed up, which is how somebody writing a negative literal in a hurry spells it) and `x=-1` (no space anywhere, a compressed style) are all left alone — only the asymmetric `x =- 1`, where the spacing groups the two operator characters together and pushes the operand away, is reported. ⚠ **The rule reads the trivia of the tree as parsed**, which is the source as the author wrote it; it draws no conclusion from what the formatter would produce, and running the formatter over the file is one of the ways to make the finding go away. Only `-`, `+` and `!` are considered: they are the unary operators whose characters also start a compound assignment (`-=`, `+=`, `!=`). A `~` or a `&` has no such reading. Compound assignments themselves are not examined, and neither is any binary operator. ⚠ There is **no fix**, deliberately: `x -= 1` and `x = -1` are both plausible readings and they are different programs, so an automatic repair would have to guess which bug it was looking at. Generated code is excluded.
